question: What criteria are used to evaluate CPU scheduling algorithms?
reference_answer: CPU utilization (percentage of time the CPU is busy), throughput (processes completed per unit time), turnaround time (submission to completion), waiting time (total time in the ready queue) and response time (request to first response). A good algorithm maximizes utilization and throughput and minimizes turnaround, waiting and response time.

gold_quotes.quote: Scheduling algorithms are evaluated based on the following criteria: 1. CPU Utilization o Percentage of time CPU is busy 2. Throughput o Number of processes completed per unit time
3. Turnaround Time o Time from submission to completion of a process 4. Waiting Time o Total time a process spends waiting in the ready queue
Time from request submission to first response
An ideal scheduling algorithm should aim to: • Maximize o CPU utilization o Throughput • Minimize

question: Why is CPU time wasted if the OS runs only one program until it finishes?
reference_answer: Without multiprogramming, a process runs until it must wait (usually for I/O); during that wait the CPU stays idle and no useful work is done. Multiprogramming lets the OS switch the CPU to another ready process so the waiting time is used productively.
key_points: CPU stays idle during the wait
multiprogramming switches the CPU to another ready process

gold_quotes.quote: During this waiting period, the CPU remains idle • CPU time is wasted and no useful work is done
Multiprogramming allows the OS to: • Switch the CPU to another ready process • Use waiting time productively

question: How is the dispatcher different from the CPU scheduler?
reference_answer: The CPU (short-term) scheduler selects a process from the ready queue and allocates the CPU to it. The dispatcher then gives control of the CPU to that selected process: it performs the context switch, switches to user mode and jumps to the right place in the user program. The time this takes is the dispatch latency.
key_points: scheduler selects a process from the ready queue
dispatcher gives the CPU to the selected process
dispatcher: context switch, user mode, jump to program location

gold_quotes.quote: The CPU scheduler (short-term scheduler): • Selects a process from the ready queue • Allocates the CPU to that process
The dispatcher is a module that: • Gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler
Performs context switch • Switches CPU to user mode • Jumps to the correct location in the user program

question: When does a CPU scheduling decision happen, and which of those cases are preemptive?
reference_answer: Scheduling decisions occur when a process (1) switches from running to waiting, (2) switches from running to ready, (3) switches from waiting to ready, or (4) terminates. Cases 1 and 4 are non-preemptive; cases 2 and 3 are preemptive.
key_points: four situations: running→waiting, running→ready, waiting→ready, terminates

gold_quotes.quote: 1. Switches from running → waiting 2. Switches from running → ready 3. Switches from waiting → ready 4. Terminates
Cases 1 and 4 → Non-preemptive • Cases 2 and 3 → Preemptive

question: Why can preemption mess up shared data, and how do operating systems avoid it?
reference_answer: Preemptive scheduling can cause race conditions: one process is preempted while updating shared data and another process then reads inconsistent data. Preemptive kernels prevent this with mutex locks and other synchronization mechanisms.
key_points: preempted while updating shared data, another reads inconsistent data

gold_quotes.quote: Problems with Preemptive Scheduling • Can cause race conditions
One process is preempted while updating shared data o Another process accesses inconsistent data
Preemptive kernels use: o Mutex locks o Other synchronization mechanisms

question: What is the difference between a program and a process?
reference_answer: A program is a passive entity, an executable file stored on disk. A process is an active entity, a program in execution. A program becomes a process when its executable is loaded into memory and execution begins, and one program can have several processes.
key_points: program: passive, executable file on disk
becomes a process when loaded into memory and run

gold_quotes.quote: A program is a passive entity o Stored on disk as an executable file • A process is an active entity o A program in execution
A program becomes a process when: • Its executable file is loaded into memory

question: What information is stored in a Process Control Block?
reference_answer: The PCB holds everything needed to manage a process: process state, program counter, CPU registers, CPU-scheduling information (priority, queue pointers), memory-management information, accounting information (CPU time used, time limits) and I/O status information (allocated devices, open files).

gold_quotes.quote: The PCB contains all information needed to manage a process
Process state o New, ready, running, waiting, terminated • Program counter o Address of next instruction to execute • CPU registers
Memory-management information o Memory allocated to the process • Accounting information
I/O status information o I/O devices allocated o List of open files

question: What happens during a context switch, and why should it be fast?
reference_answer: When the CPU switches from one process to another, the OS saves the state of the current process in its PCB and loads the saved state of the next process. Context-switch time is pure overhead because no useful work is done while switching; it depends on hardware support and PCB complexity.
key_points: save current process state in its PCB
load saved state of the next process
switch time is overhead, no useful work

gold_quotes.quote: 1. Save the state of the current process in its PCB 2. Load the saved state of the next process
Context switch time is overhead • No useful work is done during switching
When the CPU changes from executing one process to another, the system performs a context switch.

question: What happens to a child process if its parent finishes first?
reference_answer: It depends on the OS. Where a child may outlive its parent, it becomes an orphan process and is adopted by init (the system process). Some operating systems do not allow a child without a parent: when the parent terminates, all its children are terminated too (cascading termination).

gold_quotes.quote: Orphan process o Parent terminates before child o Child is adopted by init/system process
Some operating systems do not allow a child to exist without a parent. • If parent terminates → all children terminate • This is called cascading termination

question: What is the difference between a zombie process and an orphan process?
reference_answer: A zombie is a child that has terminated but whose parent has not yet called wait(). An orphan is a child whose parent terminated first; it is adopted by init.
key_points: zombie: child terminated, parent has not called wait()

gold_quotes.quote: Zombie process o Child terminates o Parent has not called wait()
Orphan process o Parent terminates before child o Child is adopted by init/system process

question: In UNIX, how does a program start a different program as a separate process?
reference_answer: It calls fork(), which creates a child process that is a duplicate of the parent. The child then calls exec(), which replaces its memory with the new program.
key_points: fork() creates a child that duplicates the parent
exec() replaces the process memory with a new program

gold_quotes.quote: fork() creates a new process • Child process is a duplicate of the parent
UNIX Example • fork() → creates child process • exec() → loads new program into child
exec() is used • Replaces the process memory with a new program

question: Why does each device controller need its own device driver?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: Each device controller is in charge of a specific device; its device driver gives the kernel a uniform interface to it, so the rest of the OS can manage I/O the same way for every device.
key_points: each controller manages a specific device
device driver gives a uniform interface to the kernel

gold_quotes.quote: Each device controller has: • Device driver • Uniform interface to kernel
Each device controller manages a specific device

question: On what basis are storage systems organized into a hierarchy?
chapter: Unit 1 – Topic 1: Introduction and Computer System Organization
reference_answer: Storage systems are organized by speed, cost and volatility; faster storage is more expensive and smaller, and caching copies frequently used data into faster storage.

gold_quotes.quote: Storage systems are organized based on: • Speed • Cost • Volatility
